headline: Linked papers claim the restricted geometric Langlands equivalence in characteristic p, plus Ramanujan bounds.
scope: The results are over curves and function fields of positive characteristic, under stated characteristic conditions on the group.
plain: The Langlands program predicts a dictionary between symmetric functions built from a field and symmetries of its equations. Over curves in characteristic p, Gaitsgory and Raskin built part of a geometric form of this dictionary. One paper claims to show no part of the dictionary is missing, under stated conditions. Other papers claim the generalized Ramanujan size bound for certain representations, including at ramified places for exceptional groups. Some further results depend on an input stated as a hypothesis.
doesNot: This does not cover number fields such as the rationals; every result here is about curves or function fields in positive characteristic.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: D. Arinkin, D. Gaitsgory, D. Kazhdan, S. Raskin, N. Rozenblyum and Y. Varshavsky, who introduced the restricted local-system stack
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims a full-support conjecture of Gaitsgory and Raskin and generic Ramanujan bounds over function fields, if the proofs hold.

explanation:
Expand the product q(1 − q)²⁴(1 − q²)²⁴(1 − q³)²⁴ and so on forever. The coefficients that come out are Ramanujan’s τ numbers. The first few are 1, −24, 252, −1472 and 4830. At the prime 2, τ(2) = −24, and 2 × 2^5.5 is about 90.5. At the prime 3, τ(3) = 252, and 2 × 3^5.5 is about 841.8. At 5 and 7 the same limit holds. Deligne proved in 1974 that this size limit holds at every prime.

That limit is the simplest case of a Ramanujan bound. In modern terms, the τ numbers come from an automorphic representation (a highly symmetric object built from a field). The generalized Ramanujan conjecture predicts tempered local pieces for generic ones, a precise form of “not too large”[3]. Temperedness means the local piece sits weakly inside the regular representation. These papers work over function fields instead of the rationals. A function field is built from a curve over a finite field, the way the rationals are built from whole numbers.

Over function fields, much was known. Drinfeld proved Ramanujan for GL₂, and Laurent Lafforgue for GLₙ[4]. Lomelí proved the generic case for split classical groups[5]. The fourth paper claims it for exceptional groups, such as G₂ and E₈, at every place[6]. That includes ramified places, where the representation is more complicated. There is no restriction on characteristic or ramification depth[6]. It builds on the third paper[7]. That paper claims temperedness at unramified places from one generic unramified place, for split adjoint simple groups[8].

The geometric side asks for more than numbers. Geometric Langlands compares two categories (collections of objects with maps between them). One side holds sheaves on the space of G-bundles over a curve. The other side holds sheaves on the space of local systems, the curve’s symmetry data. In characteristic zero, a nine-author project proved the geometric Langlands theorem[9]. In characteristic p, Gaitsgory and Raskin built an equivalence onto a union of pieces of the spectral side[10]. The open question was whether any piece is missing[10].

The fifth paper claims that no piece is missing, in two settings[10]. If correct, this proves Conjecture 1.3.10 of Gaitsgory and Raskin there[11]. One setting is a curve over the algebraic closure of a finite field. The other is any algebraically closed field, with two extra conditions on p[12]. It must be very good for the group and must not divide the Weyl group’s order. Very good excludes small primes such as 2 and 3 for E₇[13].

The argument works by contradiction. A missing piece would give a nonzero sheaf in characteristic zero that vanishes on passing to characteristic p[14]. Careful local tests with Hecke modifications show this cannot happen.

The other papers fill in pieces. One claims that a canonical Arthur filtration is defined over the rationals, as Gaitsgory, Lafforgue and Raskin conjectured[15]. Another builds Arthur enhancements, but only under the finite-level decomposition stated as a hypothesis[16]. It does not claim Arthur-packet classification or multiplicity formulas[17]. Three more construct Hecke eigensheaves with tame ramification at marked points[18].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for these papers in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked them. The papers are long, linked and rely on deep recent work. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the linked papers hold. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published. All results are over function fields in positive characteristic, and the Arthur-enhancement result is conditional.

glossary.meaning: A highly symmetric object built from a field whose numbers, like τ(p), encode arithmetic.
For a local piece of a representation, being no larger than the regular representation allows; the Ramanujan size bound.
A field built from a curve over a finite field, the way the rationals are built from whole numbers.
A collection of objects together with the maps between them.
Symmetry data of a curve: a way its loops act on a fixed vector space.
A geometric object on the space of bundles that the Hecke operators only rescale.
A point of the curve where the representation has extra complication, not the simplest local form.
